The deterioration in local, regional, national or global economic conditions could cause us to experience a reduction in deposits and new loans, an increase in the number of borrowers who default on their loans or a reduction in the value of the collateral securing loans, all of which could adversely affect the performance and financial condition of the Bank. There can be no assurance that our business and corresponding financial performance will not be adversely affected by general economic or consumer trends or events, including pandemics, public health crises, acts of terrorism, war, and political instability.</font></div><div style="height:72pt;position:relative;width:100%"><div style="bottom:0;position:absolute;width:100%"><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:center"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">19</font></div></div></div><hr style="page-break-after:always"><div style="min-height:72pt;width:100%"><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><font><br></font></div></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">Changes in market interest rates and monetary and fiscal policy may negatively affect our earnings and financial condition as well as the value of our assets.</font></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">Our earnings are largely dependent on net interest income, which is the difference between the interest yields we earn on loans, securities and other interest-earning assets and the interest rates we pay on deposits and other borrowings. Changes in general market interest rates may have a significant effect on the yields we earn and the rates we pay, thereby impacting our net interest income. In addition, the value of our assets is impacted by changes in interest rates and, as market interest rates rise, the value of our assets may decline. Further, changes in interest rates may also impact borrower demand for credit and prepayment speeds, which can have a significant impact on our net interest income. </font></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%"> The yields we earn and rates we pay are highly sensitive to many factors which are beyond our control and, accordingly, our earnings and growth are subject to the influence of economic conditions, both domestic and foreign, including inflation, recession and unemployment, and also to the influence of monetary and fiscal policies of the United States and its agencies, particularly the Federal Reserve. </font></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">The Federal Open Market Committee (the &#8220;FOMC&#8221;) sets monetary policy, such as seeking to curb inflation, maintain employment and avoid recession, through adjustments it makes to the federal funds rate, by its open-market dealings in United States government securities, by adjusting the required level of reserves for financial institutions subject to reserve requirements and by placing limitations upon savings and time deposit interest rates. The actions of the FOMC in these areas influence the growth and relative value of bank loans, investments and deposits and affect interest rates. The FOMC&#8217;s actions on the federal funds target rate generally affect the shorter end of the yield curve while the longer end of the yield curve is often impacted by the inflation expectations of investors. Banks like ours typically borrow short-term (e.g., deposits, wholesale funding) while lending long-term (e.g., loans). Our profitability depends on the spread between these rates and the change in the shape in the yield curve, such as steeper curve, flattened curve or inverted curve, may have a significant impact on our operating results, depending upon the degree to which our interest-earning assets and interest-bearing liabilities are interest rate sensitive. Therefore, the nature and timing of any future changes in yield curves and their impact on us is particularly hard to predict. While we actively monitor interest rate risk and employ interest rate risk models to inform various strategies to mitigate interest rate impact, there can be no assurance that these measures will be effective in all market environments. </font></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">We operate in a highly competitive market and face increasing competition from a variety of traditional and new financial services providers.</font></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">Our principal competitors are regional and national commercial financial institutions, as well as community banks, consumer finance companies, non-bank lenders, including &#8220;fintech&#8221; companies, credit unions and other financial institutions that operate offices in our market area and elsewhere. The larger financial institutions we compete with have greater resources that may provide them a competitive advantage by enabling them to, among other things, finance extensive advertising campaigns and to allocate their investment assets to regions of highest yield and demand. Many of the competing major commercial banks operating in our service areas offer certain services (such as trust and international banking services) that are not offered directly by us, and, by virtue of their greater total capitalization, such banks have substantially higher lending limits. We compete with these other financial institutions both in attracting deposits and making loans. We expect competition to continue to increase as a result of changes in regulation, changes in technology and product delivery systems, additional non-bank financial service providers and the accelerating pace of consolidation among financial services providers. Our profitability in large part depends upon our continued ability to compete successfully with traditional and new financial services providers, some of which maintain a physical presence in our market and others of which maintain only a virtual presence. Increased competition could require us to increase the rates we pay on deposits or lower the rates that we offer on loans, which could reduce our profitability. In addition, financial institutions like us are also experiencing intense competition from various non-banking institutions, particularly in the highly competitive Silicon Valley market where we have a branch office.</font></div><div style="height:72pt;position:relative;width:100%"><div style="bottom:0;position:absolute;width:100%"><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:center"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">20</font></div></div></div><hr style="page-break-after:always"><div style="min-height:72pt;width:100%"><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><font><br></font></div></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">Our financial performance may be negatively affected if we are unable to successfully execute on our strategic initiatives, including our growth strategy.</font></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">Our strategy is to grow our franchise organically and safely, and we have and may in the future supplement that growth with select mergers and acquisitions if they enhance our market presence and service offerings, provide economies of scale and improve profitability, among other factors. Continued growth, whether organically through branch expansion or through acquisitions, may present operating and other challenges that could adversely affect our business, financial condition and results of operations. Rapid expansion may place a strain on our administrative, operational, personnel, capital and financial resources and increase demands on our infrastructure, systems and controls. Our ability to manage growth successfully will depend on our ability to attract qualified personnel and maintain cost controls and asset quality while retaining and attracting loans and deposits on favorable terms, as well as on macro factors beyond our control, such as economic conditions and interest rate trends. If we grow too quickly and are not able to retain clients, attract qualified personnel, control costs, manage potential exposure to unknown or contingent liabilities of banks and businesses we acquire, realize expected synergies or returns on investment, efficiently allocate management&#8217;s attention, and maintain favorable asset quality, it could materially dilute our franchise value and negatively affect our financial performance.</font></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">We may need to make additional investments in systems and personnel to manage higher asset levels and loan balances, which may adversely affect earnings, shareholder returns, efficiency ratio and other metrics concerning our profitability. We may also incur significant acquisition-related expenses either during the due diligence phase of acquisition targets or during integration of the acquirees. These expenses have and may continue to negatively impact our earnings prior to achieving operational synergy. In addition, litigation risk could increase if due diligence fails to uncover exposures or other obligations and we may not achieve the targeted cost savings from acquisitions as a result.</font></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">Failure to keep pace with the rapid technological changes in the financial services industry could have an adverse effect on our competitive position and profitability.</font></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">The financial services industry is undergoing rapid technological changes, with frequent introductions of new technology-driven products and services, including artificial intelligence. The widespread adoption of new and emerging technologies, such as artificial intelligence and quantum computing, have the potential to further intensify competition and accelerate disruption in the financial services market.  Advances and changes in technology could significantly affect our businesses, financial condition, results of operations and future prospects. We face many challenges, including disruptions in the real-time payment system. Our ability to compete depends, in part, on our ability to continue to adopt technology on a timely and cost-effective basis to meet clients&#8217; real-time payment demands. The effective use of technology increases efficiency and enables financial institutions to better serve clients and reduce costs.</font></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">For example, banks like ours rely heavily on client deposits as low-cost funding sources for loans and investments. If consumers and businesses shift funds into blockchain-based payment systems such as stablecoins (especially if they are allowed to offer yield through platforms), banks could see a decline in deposits, increasing our funding costs. We also earn fees from payment processing such as ACH, wire transfers and card networks. Stablecoins that enable near-instant, low-cost transactions without intermediaries or generate interest could divert our fee income stream.</font></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">Many of our larger national bank competitors have substantially greater resources to invest in technological improvements, such as tokenized bank deposits. We may not be able to implement new technology-driven products and services effectively or be successful in marketing these products and services to our clients. Failure to keep pace successfully with technological change affecting the financial services industry could harm our ability to compete effectively and could have an adverse effect on our business, financial condition and results of operations. As these technologies improve in the future, we may be required to make significant capital expenditures in order to remain competitive, which may increase our overall expenses and have an adverse effect on our business, financial condition and results of operations.</font></div><div style="height:72pt;position:relative;width:100%"><div style="bottom:0;position:absolute;width:100%"><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:center"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">21</font></div></div></div><hr style="page-break-after:always"><div style="min-height:72pt;width:100%"><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><font><br></font></div></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">We follow a relationship-based operating model, and the ability to maintain our reputation is critical to the success of our business and failure to do so may materially adversely affect our performance.</font></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">We are a community bank, and our reputation is one of the most valuable components of our business. As such, we strive to conduct our business in a manner that enhances our reputation. This is done, in part, by recruiting, hiring and retaining bankers and other employees who share our core values of being an integral part of the communities we serve, delivering superior service to our clients and caring about our clients and employees. Furthermore, maintaining our reputation also depends on our ability to protect our brand.</font></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">However, reputation risk, or the risk to our business, earnings and capital from negative public opinion surrounding our Company, and the financial services industry generally, is inherent in our business. Negative public opinion can result from our actual or alleged conduct in any number of activities, including business and lending practices, corporate governance and acquisitions, and from actions taken by government regulators and community organizations in response to those activities. Certain events in the financial services industry, including the large-scale deposit withdrawals over a short period of time at a number of large financial institutions in the first half of 2023, led to the failure of those institutions and resulted in decreased confidence in banks among depositors, other counterparties and investors as well as significant disruption, volatility and reduced valuations of equity and other securities of banks in the capital markets. Negative public opinion can adversely affect our ability to keep and attract clients and employees and can expose us to litigation and regulatory action. Although we take steps to minimize reputational risk in dealing with our clients and communities, this risk will always be present given the nature of our business. </font></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">Moreover, some clients continue to be concerned about the extent to which their deposits are insured by the FDIC and relative strength and safety of community banks compared to much larger banks with a national footprint. Clients may withdraw deposits in an effort to ensure that the amount they have on deposit with their bank is fully insured and on deposit with a &#8220;safer&#8221; bank. The Bank offers accounts to clients that provide multi-million-dollar FDIC insurance using the IntraFi network of banks to offer reciprocal fully FDIC-insured accounts through the Insured Cash Sweep (&#8220;ICS&#8221;) or Certificate of Deposit Account Registry System (&#8220;CDARS&#8221;). Nevertheless, at June 30, 2026, the Bank estimates total uninsured deposits, excluding fully collateralized government agency deposits, represented 51.3% of total deposits. Client concerns about levels of uninsured deposits and perceived risk of potential failure of smaller community banks, like our Bank, compared to much larger banks with a national footprint could lead to decreases in deposits at our Bank. </font></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">If our reputation is negatively affected by the actions of our employees or otherwise, our business, financial condition and results of operations may be adversely affected.</font></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">Our geographic concentration in California heightens our exposure to regional economic and environmental risks.</font></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">We primarily serve businesses and individuals located in the Central Coast of California which we define as the counties of Santa Cruz, Monterey, Santa Clara and San Luis Obispo. As a result, we are exposed to risks associated with the lack of geographic diversification. Deterioration in either general economic or environmental conditions, including within our market area and in California, could also lead to temporary or permanent losses of businesses and population in our business footprints. Workforce reductions within the technology sector and declining demand from the life sciences industry could continue to reduce the demand for office space or commercial real estate development in the Bay Area and have rippling effects on the Central Coast region, including Silicon Valley. As of  June 30, 2026, 36% and 29% of our real estate loan portfolio was located in Santa Cruz and Monterey Counties, respectively, 8% in Santa Clara County, 8% in San Luis Obispo County, 13% in other California regions and 6% of our loan portfolio was located outside of California, based on the location of clients for commercial borrowers and the location of collateral for real estate loans. Any deterioration in economic conditions, in California generally and the Central Coast in particular, could result in loan delinquencies, problem assets and foreclosures. Collateral for our loans, especially real estate, are often located in areas prone to natural disasters such as earthquakes, landslides, wild fires, floods and tsunami and may decline in value, reducing clients&#8217; borrowing power and the value of assets and collateral associated with our existing loans. </font></div><div style="height:72pt;position:relative;width:100%"><div style="bottom:0;position:absolute;width:100%"><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:center"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">22</font></div></div></div><hr style="page-break-after:always"><div style="min-height:72pt;width:100%"><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><font><br></font></div></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">Risks Related to Our Lending Activities</font></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">We face lending risks, especially with respect to our small- and medium-sized business clientele and construction lending.</font></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">We primarily serve the banking and financial services needs of small- and medium-sized businesses. These businesses generally have fewer financial resources, lack capital, have less diversity in product and service offerings and lack economic scale, hence they may be more vulnerable to economic downturns and rising interest rates to service their debt and may experience substantial volatility in operating results, any of which may impair their ability as a borrower to repay a loan. In particular, a significant portion of our loan portfolio consists of adjustable-rate loans. </font></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">As of June 30, 2026, approximately 44% of our loan portfolio is subject to a rate change within the next twelve months, due to adjustable-rate structures. As interest rates rise, the debt service obligations of these borrowers increase, which reduces their available cash flow and increases the risk of default, even if their underlying business revenue remains stable.</font></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">In addition, there are risks of significant modification or loss of government funding to SBA loan programs or to not-for-profit organizations who are our clients and beneficiaries of governmental funding, thus affecting their ability to repay their loans.  </font></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">Consequently, the Bank may assume greater lending risks than other financial institutions which have a smaller concentration of those types of loans and which tend to make loans to larger businesses. Borrower defaults or borrowers&#8217; inability to make scheduled payments may result in losses that may exceed our allowances for credit losses. These risks, if they occur, may require higher than expected provisions for credit losses which, in turn, can materially impair our profitability, capital adequacy and overall financial condition.</font></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">In particular, real estate construction and land acquisition and development loans involve risks not present in other types of loans, including risks associated with construction cost overruns, project completion, general contractor credit and the ultimate sale or use of the completed construction. These risks can be exacerbated by changes in market conditions, supply chain disruptions or labor shortages, any of which may delay completion or reduce the value of the finished property. If these risks materialize, borrowers may be unable to repay their loans and collateral values may decline. The result could be increased charge-offs and higher provisions for credit losses. As of June 30, 2026, approximately 11.5% of our loan portfolio consists of construction and acquisition development loans, which exposes us to these risks to a meaningful degree.</font></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">Loans acquired through acquisitions may expose us to additional risk because they were not underwritten or originated under our credit standards.</font></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">Loans that were acquired as part of our acquisitions of other depository institutions may differ from loans that we originate in credit quality, collateral or guarantor credit support, term structure, documentation, servicing requirements and&#47;or borrower relationship history because such loans were not initially underwritten or originated in accordance with our credit standards, and we did not have long-standing relationships with many of these borrowers at the time of acquisition. We have historically evaluated, and expect to evaluate, the loan portfolio of each institution acquired as part of the diligence process prior to consummating such transaction, and believe we have established reasonable credit marks with regard to all loans acquired&#59; however, our evaluation of these loans depends in part on seller-provided information and due diligence that may not identify all existing or emerging credit, collateral, compliance, servicing or operational issues. Some acquired loans may also have experienced more-than-insignificant deterioration in credit quality since origination, increasing the likelihood of delinquency, modification, adverse risk classification, foreclosure, charge-offs or other losses.</font></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">The acquired loans were underwritten at the date of acquisition based on our credit standards, which can temporarily increase loans classified as special mention and substandard for a period of time until these loans are integrated and conform to our credit standards. While we apply our risk management processes after acquisition, we may not fully mitigate credit issues that existed prior to acquisition. In addition, integrating acquired loans into our systems, controls, credit administration and servicing processes may require significant management attention and </font></div><div style="height:72pt;position:relative;width:100%"><div style="bottom:0;position:absolute;width:100%"><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:center"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">23</font></div></div></div><hr style="page-break-after:always"><div style="min-height:72pt;width:100%"><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><font><br></font></div></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">may not be completed as effectively or timely as expected. If actual cash flow from acquired loans perform worse than expected, collateral values decline, information on acquired loan is incomplete or inaccurate, or integration is ineffective, we may incur higher delinquency rates, defaults or losses than anticipated, which could adversely affect our business, financial condition and results of operations.</font></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">We may not be able to measure and limit our credit risk adequately, may experience increased nonperforming assets and may require a material increase in our allowance for credit losses, which could adversely affect our profitability.</font></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">Our business depends on our ability to successfully measure and manage credit risk. The risk of nonpayment of loans is inherent in banking. Our loan clients may not repay their loans according to the terms of their respective loans, and the collateral securing the payment of those loans may be insufficient to assure repayment. We may experience significant credit losses, which could have a material adverse effect on our profitability.  Our management makes various assumptions and judgments about the collectability of our loans, including the creditworthiness of our borrowers and the value of the real estate and other collateral for the repayment of many of our loans.  While we seek to diversify our loan portfolio across loan types and business sectors, it is concentrated in CRE and commercial business loans. CRE and commercial business loans involve risks because the borrowers&#8217; abilities to repay the loans typically depend primarily on the successful operation of the businesses or the properties securing the loans.  At June 30, 2026, commercial real estate loans comprised 61.5% of our loan portfolio, of which 26.5% were deemed owner-occupied, while 73.5% were deemed non-owner-occupied, and 17.5% of our loan portfolio was comprised of commercial business loans and lines of credit.</font></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">We continuously strive to manage credit risk, in part, through careful loan reviews and underwriting standards. While we adhere to thorough, disciplined and prudent underwriting standards, our practices may not protect us against losses in our loan portfolio. Our credit risk management also includes maintaining an allowance for credit losses to provide for loan defaults and nonperformance. We estimate credit losses using the current expected credit loss (&#8220;CECL&#8221;) methodology, which incorporates the use of and is reliant upon reasonable and supportable forecasts of national and local economic conditions and variables, including gross domestic product and levels of unemployment. Changes in one or more of these economic variables could have an impact on our determination of the allowance for credit losses. Since the CECL methodology is more dependent on future economic forecasts, assumptions, and models than methods of reserving for loan losses under the previous accounting standards, it may result in increases and add volatility to our allowance for credit losses and future provisions for credit losses.</font></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">In addition to the use of reasonable and supportable forecasts, the allowance is also based on a variety of other factors, including historical experience, volume and types of loans, trends in classifications, volume and trends in delinquencies and non-accruals and other pertinent information. If our assumptions are wrong, our current allowance may not be sufficient to cover loan losses, and adjustments may be necessary to allow for different economic conditions or adverse developments in our loan portfolio. Material increases to our allowance for credit losses would materially decrease our earnings.</font></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">In situations where collection efforts are unsuccessful or acceptable work-out arrangements cannot be reached, we may acquire real estate or other assets through foreclosure, if any, or through other similar available remedies. When we foreclose, we are required to record the asset at its then-fair market value, which may be less than the loan balance, resulting in a loss. In such cases, the amount owed under the defaulted loan may exceed the value of assets acquired resulting in a loss requiring us to charge-off the difference. In addition, federal and state regulators periodically review our allowance for credit losses and may require us to increase the provision for credit losses or recognize further loan charge-offs based on judgments different from those of our management. </font></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">Therefore, we cannot ensure that our monitoring, procedures and policies will reduce certain lending risks or that our allowance for credit losses will be adequate to cover actual losses. If we experience greater nonpayment levels than anticipated, or we are required to increase our allowance for credit losses, our earnings and overall financial condition as well as the value of our Common Stock could be adversely affected. Our failure to effectively mitigate these risks could have an adverse effect on our business, financial condition and results of operations.</font></div><div style="height:72pt;position:relative;width:100%"><div style="bottom:0;position:absolute;width:100%"><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:center"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">24</font></div></div></div><hr style="page-break-after:always"><div style="min-height:72pt;width:100%"><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><font><br></font></div></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">Please also refer to the section titled </font><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">Management&#8217;s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations - Critical Accounting Estimates</font><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%"> under &#8220;Item 2. Financial Information&#8221; of this Registration Statement for additional discussion concerning the allowance for credit losses.  </font></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">Our focus on commercial lending subjects us to credit concentration risks.</font></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">Commercial real estate (&#8220;CRE&#8221;) and commercial and industrial loans represent 61.5% and 17.5% of our loan portfolio as of June 30, 2026, respectively.  CRE and commercial and industrial loans generally are considered riskier than single family residential loans because they have larger balances to a single borrower or group of related borrowers. CRE and commercial and industrial loans involve risks because the borrower&#8217;s ability to repay such loans usually depends upon the profitability of the borrower&#8217;s employment, business or the business that occupies the relevant real property. As a result, if the business that supports payments on a loan declines, the loan may go into default. In addition, if a property which is serving as security for a loan is foreclosed on, it often takes a long time to sell the property because there are typically few potential purchasers and the resulting value is uncertain. CRE loans and commercial and industrial loans are more susceptible to a risk of loss during a downturn in the business cycle and repayment is dependent on the successful operation and management of the associated commercial real estate. </font></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">The Board oversees and management monitors the Bank&#8217;s CRE exposures through a comprehensive risk management framework that includes regular review of CRE concentration metrics, CRE portfolio trends, third-party credit reviews and borrower-level stress testing results, scenario-based stress testing using economic scenarios consistent with those published by the Federal Reserve, established risk-based lending standards and review of internally established concentration limits. While we believe our risk management framework is generally appropriate to manage and monitor our commercial real estate concentrations, we cannot eliminate all the risks related to these loans.</font></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">Beyond concentration risk, the structural characteristics of our commercial loans, including reliance on collateral and unsecured exposures, can increase potential loss severity. Secured loans are typically backed by real estate or business assets such as receivables, inventory, and equipment, and may include personal guarantees. However, the value of this collateral often depends on the borrower&#8217;s ongoing operations and may decline significantly under adverse conditions, limiting recovery. Unsecured loans present even greater risk because repayment depends entirely on the borrower&#8217;s cash flow and business performance, leaving us with minimal recourse in the event of default. These factors compound the impact of any concentration in commercial credits.</font></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">Concentrations in non-owner-occupied commercial real estate loans expose us to heightened credit, market and regulatory risks.</font></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">A significant portion of our loan portfolio consists of non&#8209;owner-occupied CRE loans, which subject us to risks that are distinct from, and in certain respects greater than, those associated with owner&#8209;occupied CRE loans and other types of lending. </font></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">Non&#8209;owner-occupied CRE loans typically rely on cash flows generated by the underlying property, such as rental income, rather than on the operating business of the borrower occupying the property. As a result, repayment performance for these loans is more sensitive to changes in market rents, tenant demand, vacancy rates, operating expenses, capitalization rates and broader economic conditions, including interest rate volatility and inflation. Adverse developments affecting commercial real estate values or operating performance&#8212;particularly in property types experiencing structural or cyclical stress, such as office or certain retail segments&#8212;may impair borrowers&#8217; ability to service debt, reduce collateral values and increase the likelihood and severity of credit losses. CRE loans also involve greater risk because they are generally not fully amortizing over the loan period and may have a balloon payment due at maturity. A borrower&#8217;s ability to make a balloon payment typically will depend on being able to either refinance the loan or sell the underlying property in a timely manner.</font></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">In addition, non&#8209;owner-occupied CRE loans generally involve larger loan balances, higher borrower concentrations and longer workout and foreclosure timelines than other loan types. As of June 30, 2026, the largest non&#8209;owner-occupied CRE loan concentration associated with a single borrower was less than 2% of total CRE loans. In the event of borrower default, we may be required to pursue foreclosure or other remedies, which can be time&#8209;consuming, expensive and the value of the underlying collateral is subject to market conditions at the time of </font></div><div style="height:72pt;position:relative;width:100%"><div style="bottom:0;position:absolute;width:100%"><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:center"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">25</font></div></div></div><hr style="page-break-after:always"><div style="min-height:72pt;width:100%"><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><font><br></font></div></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">disposition. If collateral values have declined and the borrower no longer performs according to the terms of the loan agreement, we may incur charge&#8209;offs and losses beyond amounts estimated in our allowance for credit losses.</font></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">Furthermore, federal banking regulators have issued guidance for banks with CRE loan balances (which, as defined by applicable regulatory guidelines, exclude owner-occupied CRE) that exceed 300% of its total risk-based capital and that have increased by 50% or more during the prior 36 months may be subject to heightened supervisory scrutiny. For these purposes, the regulatory classification of CRE, which is based primarily on the underlying collateral rather than the business purpose of the loans, consist of non-owner-occupied loans secured by non-farm non-residential properties, multifamily properties, and loans for construction and land development. As of June 30, 2026, our total CRE loans, based on the regulatory classification as just described, were approximately $1.4 billion of total CRE loans and represented approximately 362% of the Bank&#8217;s total risk-based capital, compared to approximately $774 million of total CRE loans and approximately 363% of the Bank&#8217;s total risk-based capital as of June 30, 2023, prior to our merger with 1</font><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:6.5pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%;position:relative;top:-3.5pt;vertical-align:baseline">st</font><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%"> Capital Bancorp in 2024. Total non-owner-occupied CRE loans (based on regulatory definition) have increased by approximately $577 million, or 75%, during the prior 36 months. This increase can be attributed in large part to CRE loans acquired in the merger with 1</font><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:6.5pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%;position:relative;top:-3.5pt;vertical-align:baseline">st</font><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%"> Capital Bancorp on October 1, 2024, which totaled approximately $330 million as of the acquisition date, based on the regulatory definition of the underlying collateral of the loans rather than the purpose of the loans. </font></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">If our concentration continues to exceed the regulatory thresholds described above, we may be subject to regulatory scrutiny or be required to maintain higher capital levels or implement enhanced risk-management practices, which could increase our costs or limit our ability to grow this portion of our loan portfolio. Should we have a number of defaults on these types of loans, such defaults could have an adverse impact on the financial condition and results of operations of the Bank.</font></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">The Board oversees and management monitors the Bank&#8217;s CRE exposures through a comprehensive risk management framework that includes risk-based lending standards, internally established product and geographic concentration limits, annual evaluations of income-producing property loans, third-party credit reviews, borrower-level stress testing of non-owner-occupied CRE exposures, and scenario-based stress testing using economic scenarios consistent with those published by the Federal Reserve.</font></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">Although management and the Board actively monitor non&#8209;owner-occupied CRE exposures and believe our risk management framework is generally appropriate to manage our non-owner-occupied CRE exposures, there can be no assurance that these measures will be sufficient to mitigate risks related to these loans, including risks arising from adverse economic conditions, real estate market disruptions or regulatory scrutiny. Any material deterioration in the performance or value of our non&#8209;owner-occupied CRE loan portfolio could have a disproportionate adverse effect on our asset quality, earnings, capital levels and ability to grow or return capital to shareholders.</font></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">Please also see the section titled &#8220;</font><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">Management&#8217;s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations - Loan Portfolio</font><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">&#8221; under &#8220;Item 2. Financial Information&#8221; of this Registration Statement for more information concerning our non-owner-occupied commercial real estate loan exposures.</font></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">Adverse changes in the real estate market or economy in our market area could lead to higher levels of problem loans and charge-offs, adversely affecting our earnings and financial condition.</font></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">As of June 30, 2026, approximately 89% of our loans, measured by dollar volume, are secured by a senior lien on real estate collateral. Nearly all of the real estate securing these loans is located in California, primarily in Santa Cruz and Monterey counties and to a lesser extent Santa Clara and San Luis Obispo counties. Real estate values are generally affected by factors such as&#58; </font></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;padding-left:36pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:-18pt"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">&#8226;</font><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%;padding-left:14.5pt">the socioeconomic conditions of the area where real estate collateral is located&#59; </font></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;padding-left:36pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:-18pt"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">&#8226;</font><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%;padding-left:14.5pt">fluctuations in interest rates&#59; </font></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;padding-left:36pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:-18pt"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">&#8226;</font><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%;padding-left:14.5pt">property and income tax laws&#59;</font></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;padding-left:36pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:-18pt"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">&#8226;</font><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%;padding-left:14.5pt">local zoning ordinances governing the manner in which real estate may be used&#59; and </font></div><div style="height:72pt;position:relative;width:100%"><div style="bottom:0;position:absolute;width:100%"><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:center"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">26</font></div></div></div><hr style="page-break-after:always"><div style="min-height:72pt;width:100%"><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><font><br></font></div></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;padding-left:36pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:-18pt"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">&#8226;</font><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%;padding-left:14.5pt">federal, state and local environmental regulations. </font></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">Declines in real estate values could significantly reduce the value of the real estate collateral securing our loans, increasing the likelihood of defaults. Moreover, if the value of real estate collateral declines to a level that is not adequate to provide security for the underlying loans, we will need to make additional provisions for credit losses which will reduce our profits. At present, office commercial real estate markets, particularly in urban and suburban areas, are experiencing weakness, which may contribute to further declines in collateral values and increase default risk for loans secured by such properties. In addition, if a borrower defaults on a real estate secured loan, we may be forced to foreclose on the property, incur charge-offs to the extent the value of the foreclosed property is insufficient to cover the unpaid balance of the loan and carry the foreclosed property as a nonearning asset, which may reduce net interest income and impact other measures of our profitability. Furthermore, our ability to foreclose on real estate collateral may be limited by environmental liabilities. If we foreclose on a property that is contaminated, we could be held liable to a governmental entity or a third party for property damage, personal injury or for investigation and cleanup costs under federal or state laws, regardless of whether we caused the contamination.  In addition, if we are the owner or former owner of a contaminated site, we may be subject to claims by third parties based on damages and costs resulting from environmental contamination emanating from the property. These costs could exceed the value of the property and adversely affect our financial condition, liquidity and results of operations.</font></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%"> We also rely on appraisals and other valuation techniques when originating real estate loans and recording other real estate owned (&#8220;OREO&#8221;) acquired through foreclosure. Appraisals represent estimates at a point in time and may not reflect subsequent changes in market conditions. Inaccurate valuations could lead to understated loan impairments or misstatement of OREO values, requiring higher provisions for credit losses and adversely affecting our financial condition.</font></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">Risks Related to Our Operations</font></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">We face risks related to our operational, technological and organizational infrastructure.</font></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">Our ability to grow and compete is dependent on the Bank&#8217;s ability to build or acquire the necessary operational and technological infrastructure and to manage the cost of that infrastructure as we expand. In our case, operational risk can manifest in many ways, such as errors related to failed or inadequate processes, faulty or disabled computer systems, fraud by employees or outside persons and exposure to external events. In addition, the Bank is heavily dependent on the strength and capability of our technology systems used both to interface with clients and to manage internal financial and other systems. Our ability to develop and deliver new products that meet the needs of our existing clients and attract new ones depends on the functionality of our technology systems. Any capital loans by a bank holding company to any of its subsidiary banks are subordinate in right of payment to depositors and to certain other indebtedness of such subsidiary banks. In the event of a bank holding company&#8217;s bankruptcy, any commitment by the bank holding company to a federal bank regulatory agency to maintain the capital of a subsidiary bank will be assumed by the bankruptcy trustee and entitled to a priority of payment. Accordingly, we could be required to provide financial assistance to the Bank if it experiences financial distress.</font></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">A capital injection may be required at a time when our resources are limited, and we may be required to borrow the funds or raise capital to make the required capital injection. Any loan by a bank holding company to its subsidiary bank is subordinate in right of payment to deposits and certain other indebtedness of such subsidiary bank. In the event of a bank holding company&#8217;s bankruptcy, the bankruptcy trustee will assume any commitment by the holding company to a federal bank regulatory agency to maintain the capital of a subsidiary bank. Moreover, bankruptcy law provides that claims based on any such commitment will be entitled to a priority of payment over the claims of the holding company&#8217;s general unsecured creditors, including the holders of any note obligations. Thus, any borrowing by a bank holding company for the purpose of making a capital injection to a subsidiary bank may become more difficult and expensive relative to other corporate borrowings.</font></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">We face a risk of noncompliance and enforcement action with the BSA and other anti-money laundering statutes and regulations.</font></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">The USA PATRIOT Act and BSA require financial institutions to maintain programs to prevent financial institutions from being used for money laundering and terrorist activities. If such activities are detected, financial institutions are obligated to file suspicious activity reports with the U.S. Department of the Treasury&#8217;s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network. These rules require financial institutions to establish procedures for identifying and verifying the identity of clients seeking to open new financial accounts. Failure to comply with these regulations could result in fines or sanctions. Although we have developed policies and procedures designed to assist in compliance with these laws and regulations, no assurance can be given that these policies and procedures will be effective in preventing violations of these laws and regulations. Failure to maintain and implement adequate programs to combat money laundering and terrorist financing could also have significant reputational consequences for us. Any of these circumstances could have an adverse effect on our business, financial condition and results of operations.</font></div><div style="height:72pt;position:relative;width:100%"><div style="bottom:0;position:absolute;width:100%"><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:center"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">31</font></div></div></div><hr style="page-break-after:always"><div style="min-height:72pt;width:100%"><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><font><br></font></div></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">Our use of third-party vendors and our other ongoing third-party business relationships are subject to increasing regulatory requirements and attention.</font></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">We regularly use third-party vendors in our business, and we rely on some of these vendors for critical functions including, but not limited to, our core processing function. The process for determining whether an allowance for credit losses is required involves complex, subjective judgments about the future financial performance and liquidity of the issuer, any collateral underlying the security, and our intent and ability to hold the security for a sufficient period of time to allow for any anticipated recovery in fair value, in order to assess the probability of receiving all contractual principal and interest payments on the security. Our non-brokered deposits are based on a relationship with the client rather than a contractual agreement. We may also be forced, as a result of withdrawals of deposits, to raise deposit rates in an attempt to attract new deposits, which would adversely affect our results of operations.</font></div><div style="height:72pt;position:relative;width:100%"><div style="bottom:0;position:absolute;width:100%"><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:center"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">32</font></div></div></div><hr style="page-break-after:always"><div style="min-height:72pt;width:100%"><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><font><br></font></div></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">Liquidity risk could impair our ability to fund operations and meet our obligations.</font></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">Liquidity is essential to our business. The program is tested periodically, although no business continuity or disaster recovery program can ensure continuity or recovery under all circumstances. We may also decide to discontinue existing products, business initiatives, services or partnerships due to technological enhancements that enable better alternatives, lack of customer acceptance, unprofitability or any other reason at our discretion. These initiatives may require significant management attention and financial, operational, technological, compliance, and other resources and may expose us to additional operational, legal, regulatory, reputational, and strategic risks. Their success depends on a number of factors, including market acceptance, effective execution, adequate staffing and expertise, appropriate systems and controls, third-party performance, and compliance with applicable laws and regulations. We may not achieve expected implementation timelines, revenue or profitability targets, or other anticipated benefits, and any such initiative may increase the complexity of our operations and place additional demands on our risk management framework and internal controls. If we are unable to successfully evaluate, develop, implement, manage, or, where appropriate, discontinue these initiatives, our business, financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected. </font></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">Litigation and regulatory actions, including possible enforcement actions, could subject us to significant fines, penalties, judgments, or other requirements resulting in increased expenses or restrictions on our business activities.</font></div><div style="margin-bottom:9pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:18pt"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">From time to time, in the normal course of business, we have in the past been and may in the future be named as a defendant in various legal actions, arising in connection with our current and&#47;or prior business activities.
